source_title: A month of calmer project handoffs
source_credit: Original fictional interview written for this software demonstration; no real customer

brand.name: Small Studio Fieldnotes
brand.voice: Clear, practical and warm. Distinguish personal operating choices from measured outcomes. Do not invent savings or client results.
brand.footer: Fictional demonstration edition. Before sending a real edition, configure the client's sender details and preference/unsubscribe fields in its existing email platform.

segments.heading: Start the handoff before the project ends
segments.text: I start a handoff note when a project begins, not on its final afternoon. The note has three headings: what we are making, where the working files live, and what the next person needs to decide. I update those headings as decisions change. That is my working habit, not a promise about how every team should operate.
segments.notes: Fictional speaker. Preserve the distinction between a personal workflow and a measured result.

segments.heading: Make the next action explicit
segments.text: My closing note names one next action and the person expected to take it. 'Please review' is too vague for my own projects. I prefer 'Choose the headline before the layout pass.' When nobody owns that choice yet, I write that the owner is still unassigned rather than guessing.
segments.notes: Example phrases are original demonstration text, not customer quotes.

segments.heading: Separate decisions from discussion
segments.text: I keep discussion notes and current decisions in different sections. A conversation can contain several abandoned options. The current decision section says which option we chose and why. Someone joining later can find the present answer without treating every suggestion as an instruction.
segments.notes: No claim of productivity improvement has been measured.

segments.heading: Leave a route back to the source
segments.text: For a decision that depends on a document, I record its title and the relevant section. If the document changes, the note needs another look. A link alone does not tell the next person which version or paragraph informed the choice.
segments.notes: Research task for a real client: add its actual document/version convention.

segments.heading: Choose useful feedback prompts
segments.text: Before sharing a draft, I say what kind of feedback would help. An early outline needs feedback on structure. A nearly finished page needs comments on wording and missing information. I also say which parts are intentionally unfinished, so placeholders are not mistaken for final decisions.
segments.notes: This is an editorial example, not a universal review rule.

segments.heading: Keep a readable revision trail
segments.text: After an edit, I leave a short note explaining the change. 'Replaced the opening example because it used the wrong audience' is useful to me later. I retain the previous version so that restoring a passage is a deliberate choice rather than a reconstruction from memory.
segments.notes: The application preserves full revisions; this fictional advice is separately sourced to the demo interview.

segments.heading: Package working files, not just a preview
segments.text: A preview is useful for a quick read, but my handoff also includes the editable text and the original inputs. I identify the current version in the package. I avoid naming a folder 'final-final' because the name does not explain what changed or which revision another person has opened.
segments.notes: Demonstration of a source-bound practical issue; no external facts required.

segments.heading: Distinguish prepared from delivered
segments.text: I treat a prepared delivery and a completed delivery as different states. A file on my desk has not reached a client. When I use a publishing platform, I keep its job or message reference with my handoff note. A planned date belongs on the calendar, but the date alone is not a delivery receipt.
segments.notes: External delivery in this app is operator-recorded, never inferred from exporting a file.
